title: Why Do Your Ears POP on a Plane? ✈️
description:
Your plane takes off... and something in your head goes POP. Behind your eardrum is a tiny pocket of air. As the cabin pressure drops on the climb, that air swells and pushes the eardrum out, until a small tube that runs to the back of your nose (the eustachian tube) lets the extra out. Subscribe for a new strange question every day.

Landing is harder. Now the pocket is short of air, the eardrum gets sucked inward, and that same suction holds the tube shut. Swallowing or yawning makes a little muscle pull it open. Babies can't do that on purpose, but pediatricians say crying can open the tube too.
